urls.description: Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have stimulated discussions about medical superintelligence, yet how to define and evaluate this aspiration remains unclear. We discuss how AI technologies can contribute to more effective care, introducing six interdependent dimensions of medical intelligence to frame contributions of AI to healthcare delivery. As AI capabilities and their integration into clinical workflows advance, improving the quality of care will require more than superhuman performance on isolated tasks. It will require systems that harness AI, independently and in collaboration with humans, to surpass today’s strongest human-led health systems in integrated medical reasoning across the full arc of care. Realising their value will require understanding how these capabilities complement existing medical intelligence and combining them effectively to improve the quality and accessibility of care.
urls.title: Medical superintelligence: foundations and aspirations

Dylan Patel explains why he thinks substrates are "the biggest bottleneck of all the bottlenecks," ahead of memory and optics, and bigger than power, land, or tools

“Yes, I think on the semiconductor side, the biggest constraint, of course, besides memory, is substrates, PCB materials, substrate materials, all of these components were severely under-invested in. Much of the supply chains that create the materials in Japan, those firms are sort of a lot more conservative and unwilling to invest heavily in capacity."

"And so we’ve seen, you know, tremendous bottlenecks there in terms of what can be made over the next two years, you know, both for accelerators as well as CPUs and every other component in the supply chain. So substrates is, I think, the biggest bottleneck of all the bottlenecks, including, you know, land, power, shell, semiconductors, tools."

"I’d say the next bottleneck would be, of course, memory. And then following that, there’s a lot of bottlenecks around the desire to ramp optics to a really, really large degree, right, with co-package optics or near-package optics. There’s humongous constraints in ramping that. You know, we just simply cannot ramp, you know, even if everyone wanted to do CPO in 2028, or even one major company wanted to do CPO in 2028, they could not satisfy their volumes in terms of lasers, in terms of fiber attach, in terms of all these different components that go into it.”
_______
